podcast.title: Solidarity with Woodstock '94 Audience (August 1994)
podcast.body: During Nine Inch Nails' performance at Woodstock '94, Trent Reznor and the entire band rolled around in the mud and became "absolutely filthy" as a show of solidarity with the audience, who were already tired, dirty, and wet from heavy rain. "In a show of solidarity, Trent and the whole band rolled around in the mud and got absolutely filthy."

podcast.title: Struggles with Addiction and Recovery (1994-2001)
podcast.body: Following "The Downward Spiral," Trent fell into a deep, five-year depression, self-medicating with alcohol, coke, and heroin, leading to suicidal thoughts. His grandmother's death exacerbated his struggles. He recorded "The Fragile" while "on a pretty slippery slope," believing himself cured upon its release, but relapsed for a "year and a half testing to see how low I could go." He described this period as "a miserable time of being sick and sweating and vomiting and hiding and just being awful," and considered it a "miracle" he didn't die. In 2001, after the last tour, he committed to intensive rehab, learning humility and self-care, and confronting his creative fears about writing sober. "My soul had been crushed by being an alcoholic and an addict. And there was no denying at that point."

podcast.title: Woodstock '94 Performance and Legacy (August 1994)
podcast.body: Trent Reznor, as the frontman of Nine Inch Nails, led a performance at Woodstock '94 that solidified his position as one of the most important new rock artists of the 1990s. Despite pre-show chaos involving a power line striking their bus, he and the band deliberately rolled in the mud on stage in solidarity with the audience, creating a memorable and impactful set. "The performance that night solidified Trent's position as one of the most important new rock artists of the 1990s."

podcast.title: Plagiarism Suit by Mark Anofrio (1997-1998)
podcast.body: Trent Reznor was accused by LA musician Mark Anofrio on August 18, 1997, of stealing six songs, including five from "The Downward Spiral" (1994) and "Burn." Anofrio claimed he had sent recorded material, under the name Elephant Man, to Reznor's home. The case, after delays and Anofrio dropping claims on some songs, was eventually dismissed by a federal judge on December 1, 1998. "On August 18th, 1997, he was notified that an LA musician named Mark Anofrio had accused Trent of stealing six of his songs."

podcast.title: Struggle with Addiction (Post-2001)

He described his soul as "crushed" and realized he faced a choice between death or recovery. This moment of clarity led him to commit to overcoming his addiction and turning his life around. "And my soul had been crushed by being an alcoholic and an addict."

podcast.title: Songwriting Credit on "Old Town Road" (2019)
podcast.body: Trent Reznor holds the record for the most weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart due to his songwriting credit on Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road." His involvement stemmed from the song's beat sampling the instrumental track "34 Ghosts 4" from Nine Inch Nails' 2008 album "Ghosts I–IV," with Reznor granting permission for the sample and receiving credit alongside his songwriting partner Atticus Ross. "Trent listened to Old Town Road and declared it to be unbelievably catchy, so he said, yeah, go ahead and use it, but I need a songwriting credit, which is very reasonable."

podcast.title: "Eat Your Heart Out, Steve" Message
podcast.body: Following the commercial and critical success of the "Broken" EP, which won a Grammy, Trent Reznor included a hidden message for TVT president Steve Gottlieb. At the 32-second mark of track 98, an unlisted track called "Physical," Trent can be heard whispering, "eat your heart out, Steve." This subtle act of defiance was his personal vindication against the label executive who had called his debut album an "abortion." "It's there, but you'll eat headphones to hear it properly."

podcast.title: Early Career and Studio Work
podcast.body: Trent initially considered a job making synthesizers but instead moved to Cleveland, working in a music store that sold many keyboards. This allowed him to experiment with the latest gear. Later, in late 1987 or early 1988, he found work at The Right Track recording studio in Cleveland, performing menial tasks like gathering cables and cleaning toilets. During the quiet hours, usually between 3 and 8 AM, he had the studio to himself to develop what would become the first Nine Inch Nails album. "By this time, late 87 early 1988, Trent had found work in Cleveland in a recording studio called The Right Track."

podcast.title: Frustration and Evolution with "Broken"
podcast.body: While battling TVT Records, Trent felt immense frustration, amplified by the unexpected success of Nine Inch Nails, which made him uncomfortable. Facing the prospect of being unable to release new music due to the legal dispute, and dealing with personal crises, he channeled these feelings into the "Broken" EP. He aimed for a more aggressive sound, experimenting with real guitars and drums, having previously only used machine buttons. He also harbored a desire to "commercially destroy" Nine Inch Nails with this record. "I also was faced with the prospect of it all being over because I couldn't put in music anymore because of this f***ing record label that I was on, and I was on some personal crises at the same time, so it all got focused into that little EP of hate."

podcast.title: Independent Release Strategy
podcast.body: Trent Reznor "went rogue" by releasing music independently, often for free, through his own company, The Null Corporation. This strategy, applied to albums like *Year Zero* (2007), *The Ghosts 1-4 Collection* (2008), and *The Slip* (2008), challenged traditional major label models and highlighted the viability of independent distribution. "It didn't help the majors case when artists like Trent Rezner went rogue, releasing all kinds of music not only as an independent, but also for free. His year zero album from 2007, The Ghosts 1-4 Collection from 2008, and The Slip also from 2008 were all released independently through Trent's company called The Null Corporation."

Just before Trent left for England to record the debut album, he reconnected with an ex-girlfriend named Patty, only to discover she had met someone else, gotten pregnant, and was getting married. Legend also suggests the song might have been inspired by a relationship with a cocaine pipe. "So a lot of anguish and heartbreak that we hear in that song is completely genuine."

"the basis for everything he's done and for what nine-inch nails has become is the piano. A big chunk of nine-inch nails tracks start as piano compositions because of his classical training. He's just more comfortable sitting at a piano than anywhere else."

podcast.title: Renting Manson Murder House (10,050 Cielo Drive)
podcast.body: In July 1992, Trent rented a secluded house at 10,050 Cielo Drive in Benedict Canyon, Los Angeles, to record "The Downward Spiral." He only learned after signing that this was the site of the Manson family murders in 1969, where Sharon Tate and others were brutally killed. Despite being "freaked out" and trying to find an alternative, he moved his studio gear into the house, specifically the room where Tate and Jay Sebring died. He named his temporary studio "Le Pig." "It was apparently only after the rental agreement was signed, the Trent learned of the house's history. 10,050 C.L.O. Drive is where the first of the Manson family murders took place."

podcast.title: Sampling Nightclubbing
podcast.body: In 1994, Trent Reznor sampled the opening beats of Iggy Pop's "Nightclubbing" from "The Idiot." He loaded the beats into a Macintosh computer, inverted the waveform, and added effects to create a new sound, demonstrating innovative use of existing material. "In 1994, Trent Rezner took those beats, loaded them into a Macintosh computer, turned the wave form upside down, added a few extra effects, and got this."

podcast.title: Secret Recording as 1000 Homo DJs
podcast.body: During his contract dispute with TVT Records, Trent Reznor secretly recorded vocals on a cover of Black Sabbath's "Supernaut" for the Ministry spin-off band 1000 Homo DJs. There is a dispute whether his vocals actually appear on most versions; only versions specifically labeled "Trent Rezner Vocal Version" feature his voice, otherwise it's Al Jourgensen's voice with distortion. "The result was that Trent had to record secretly and under fake names. One such recording was a ministry spin-off band called 1000 homo DJs."

podcast.title: Signature Piano Sound and Manipulation
podcast.body: Trent Reznor frequently uses an old upright piano to sample its sounds, which he then treats and manipulates into new forms. He has developed a distinctive piano sound that he continues to use in his movie soundtracks, often integrating this element into chaotic and noisy compositions. "He often uses an old upright model to sample its sounds and then treat and manipulate them into something else. In fact, Trent developed a signature piano sound that he uses to this day in movie sound tracks that he composes."

podcast.body: As the creator of Nine Inch Nails' "34 Ghosts 4," Trent Reznor, along with Atticus Ross, received songwriting credits for Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road" after a quiet negotiation. podcast.title: TVT Records Contract Dispute
podcast.body: After signing with TVT Records, the label's owner, Steve Gottlieb, disliked Trent's debut album "Pretty Hate Machine" for being too heavy and dark. When Steve demanded a more commercially palatable follow-up, Trent refused and sought release from his contract. TVT denied his request, putting him in "limbo for a couple of years" and forbidding him from recording or releasing new music, even allowing "Pretty Hate Machine" to go out of print. This forced Trent to record secretly under fake names. "But when Steve demanded that the follow up record be more commercially palatable, Trent not so respectfully declined and demanded that he be led out of his contract."

podcast.title: Taming Noise
podcast.body: Since the 1980s, Trent Reznor has been actively experimenting with how to harness and control noise within his music. His approach to sound design, heavily reliant on distortion and feedback, was fundamental to the creation of albums like "The Downward Spiral." xref.title: Supergroup Lineup and Origins (1994-2001)
xref.body: Tapeworm was conceived as a side project during Nine Inch Nails' "The Downward Spiral" sessions in 1994, intended as a collaborative effort for Danny Lohner and Charlie Clouser. It evolved to include a star-studded lineup: Trent Reznor, Maynard James Keenan (Tool), producer Alan Molder, Atticus Ross, Phil Anselmo and Rex Brown (Pantera), Page Hamilton (Helmet), Toni Halliday (Curve), Tommy Victor (Ministry), and drummer Josh Freese, with at least an album's worth of material recorded by 2001. "If you're Trent Rezner, Danny Loaner and Charlie Closer from his live band, Maynard James Keenan from Tool, producer Alan Molder and Atticus Ross. I mean, wow, awesome, right? The idea for tapeworm went as far back as the sessions for the downward spiral in 1994. Tapeworm was designed as something to which Danny and Charlie could contribute as equals. This idea evolved into something pretty cool. Maynard was brought in, Phil and Salmo from Pantera, Paige Hamilton from Helmut, Tony Haliday from a cool band called Curve, Tommy Victor from Ministry, drummer Josh Freeze. And then in 2001, Alan Molder apparently helped record at least an album's worth of stuff."

xref.body: Trent Reznor accidentally contributed to Lil Nas X becoming a major pop star when the latter used a remixed instrumental track from Nine Inch Nails' "Ghosts I–IV" for his hit song "Old Town Road." "And he accidentally turned Lil Nas X into one of the biggest pop stars in the planet."

xref.title: Industrial Breakthrough
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails, led by Trent Reznor, emerged as an even bigger industrial group than Ministry, winning a Grammy Award in 1992. Their success, including regular rotation on Alt Rock stations, represented a significant breakthrough for industrial music from the fringes into the mainstream in the early 90s. "But they lost out to an even bigger industrial group, Trent Rezner and Nine-inch Nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Industrial Music Scene Influence
xref.body: This band was very important to the industrial music scene and a favorite of Trent Reznor. Peter Christopherson, a member, collaborated on the original video art project for Nine Inch Nails' "Broken" EP. "Two bands very important to the industrial music scene and two favorites of Trent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Contemporary Artists
xref.body: The album *Loveless* had a profound and widespread impact, blowing away musicians such as Trent Reznor, Billy Corgan, Robert Smith, Courtney Love, and The Edge of U2. Its influence far exceeded its commercial sales, cementing its status as a seminal work in alternative music and being frequently cited by contemporary bands as an inspiration. "Everyone from Trent Resner to Billy Corgan to Robert Smith to Courtney Love to the edge of YouTube were blown away by what they heard on that album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Ministry was a significant influence on Trent Reznor's musical direction, particularly their "rage and fury." This inspiration contributed to Trent's shift from his earlier techno-pop influences towards the harder, more sinister industrial sound that defined Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Front 242 was a key influence on Trent Reznor, specifically their "rage and fury." This inspiration helped guide Trent's evolving sound towards the more aggressive, industrial style adopted by Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Skinny Puppy was a profound influence on Trent Reznor, particularly their sound's "rage and fury." They were instrumental in his shift away from techno-pop and towards the more aggressive, industrial direction that characterized early Nine Inch Nails material, directly inspiring his first song in this new style, "Down In It." "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Depeche Mode, along with The Human League and OMD, greatly influenced Trent Reznor with their use of synthesizers and drum machines. Their sound was deemed "really cool" by Trent, shaping his musical taste and aspirations. Steve Gottlieb, president of TVT Records, even expected Nine Inch Nails to be an "edgier Depeche Mode" upon signing them. "But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor and Nine Inch Nails
xref.body: Skinny Puppy's intense and heavy sound, particularly from songs like "Dig It," directly inspired Trent Reznor to re-evaluate his work in techno-pop and subsequently form Nine Inch Nails to emulate their style. "It was songs like that, which made Trent Rezner rethink what he was doing in his Tecno Pop bands, and ultimately he formed 9-inch-dales to emulate Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Interviewed by Host
xref.body: Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails was among the artists interviewed by the host over the years. "I've had the privilege of talking to a ton of really cool people over the years...Trent Rezner."

xref.title: Largest Indie Band Status
xref.body: Around the time Trent Reznor was gaining attention, Depeche Mode could argue they were the biggest indie band in the world. They were one of the first signings to Mute Records, an independent label founded in 1978. "Around the same time the Trent Rezner was attracting his first bit of attention, a British electro group could argue that they were in fact the biggest Indie band in the world."

xref.title: Legal Defense by Charles B. Ortoner
xref.body: Trent Reznor was defended in his plagiarism lawsuit by Charles B. Ortoner, a New York-based lawyer specializing in such cases. Ortoner's successful defense led to the case being thrown out by a federal judge. "As a point of interest, Trent's lawyer in the case was Charles B. Ortoner, who's based out of New York."

xref.title: Ministry's Outtakes Project
xref.body: 1000 Homo DJs served as a "goofy side project" initiated by Al Jourgensen of Ministry to release material, specifically Ministry outtakes, while maintaining a clear separation from the main band. The project involved all contributing members adopting fake names for their credits, including Jourgensen (Lux/Buck Satan), Paul Barker (Pan/Officer Aggro), and William Rieflin (We Willy Riefer), and famously included uncredited vocals from Trent Reznor. "He started a goofy side project called 1000 Home Old DJs as a way of releasing some ministry outtakes while keeping things separate from his main band."

xref.body: Music eventually led Trent Reznor to the big city of Cleveland, where he secured jobs at a music store and then a recording studio, setting the stage for the Nine Inch Nails story. "But music kept drawing his attention away to the big city of Cleveland. He moved there, got a job at a music store, then a recording studio, and then, you know, the nine-inch nail story after that, right?"

xref.body: A track by Nine Inch Nails is played as a "contribute to Hugh Lacane, the inventor of the earliest form of keyboard synthesizer." xref.body: Marilyn Manson's association with Trent Reznor in the late 1990s was noted as unhelpful during Reznor's struggle with heavy drinking, cocaine, and heroin addiction. "But the late 90s, he was a mess, a full-blown junkie, and hanging around with Marilyn Manson didn't help matters much either."

xref.title: Nine Inch Nails as Opener
xref.body: In the spring of 1990, Nine Inch Nails opened for Peter Murphy during a tour. This provided an early touring platform for Trent Reznor's band, during which they performed a cover of a Queen song and experienced growing frustrations with their record label, TVT. "In the spring of 1990, Trent went on the road as the opener for Peter Murphy and one of the songs in the nine-inch nail set list at that time was this cover of an old song by Queen."

xref.title: Notable Contributors to Music
xref.body: Over the years, Jackalope's music featured contributions from a range of distinguished artists, including members of Sloan and Monster Magnet, Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails (who also co-produced), Alex Lifeson of Rush, and the three members named Don from Sons of Freedom. xref.title: Nothing Records – Vanity Boutique Label
xref.body: Trent Reznor's Nothing Records was created by Interscope, a subsidiary of Universal, as a special vanity boutique label. This arrangement gave Trent Reznor extra creative control, allowing him to pursue, sign, develop, and produce talent independently. It exemplifies how major labels can establish indie-looking imprints for significant artists. "This gave Trent some extra creative control and allowed him to pursue, sign, develop and produce talent on his own."

xref.title: Ongoing Collaboration with Trent Reznor
xref.body: The experience with Tapeworm, despite not resulting in a release, must have been positive, as Atticus Ross has worked on every Nine Inch Nails album since "With Teeth" (2005). "Atticus has worked on every 9-H nails album since with Teeth in 2005."

xref.title: Origin of the Name "Nine Inch Nails"
xref.body: The name "Nine Inch Nails" does not carry any special meaning or symbolism, despite potential rumors. Trent Reznor simply came up with it while doodling names and liked how it sounded, so he decided to keep it. "Well, nowhere really. It doesn't mean anything special, despite any rumors that you may have heard."

xref.title: Personal Struggles and Grandmother's Death (Mid-Late 1990s)
xref.body: Trent Reznor suffered from depression and a social anxiety disorder. The death of his grandmother, who raised him, profoundly affected him, leading to heavy drinking, cocaine use, and ultimately heroin addiction by the late 1990s. His association with Marilyn Manson during this period was also noted as unhelpful. "The death of his grandmother, the woman who raised him really messed him up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Piano as the Foundational Compositional Instrument
xref.body: A significant portion of Nine Inch Nails' tracks originate as piano compositions, directly stemming from Trent Reznor's classical training. The piano serves as the fundamental basis for the band's unique sound and overall artistic direction, providing a core structure to their complex arrangements. "A big chunk of nine-inch nails tracks start as piano compositions because of his classical training. He's just more comfortable sitting at a piano than anywhere else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-High School Education and Wilderness Living
xref.body: After graduating high school, Trent Reznor enrolled in a computer course at a nearby college in Meadville (population 15,000). However, he dropped out and spent about a year living in the woods with his father before music drew his attention to Cleveland. "The train graduated from high school. He enrolled in a computer course at nearby college in Medville, which had a population of 15,000. But he dropped out and went to live in the woods with his father for about a year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Primary Inspiration for Trent Reznor
xref.body: The Human League served as Trent Reznor's "true inspiration" for becoming a musician. Their use of synthesizers and drum machines profoundly influenced him, more so than the punk bands of the era, shaping his early appreciation for electronic music. "Trent's true inspiration for becoming a musician was believe it or not, the human league."

xref.title: Rehab and Detox (Early 2000s)
xref.body: After his overdose in London, Trent Reznor eventually decided to confront his addictions. He checked into a rehab facility in New Orleans and underwent a severe detox. "He checked into a rehab facility in New Orleans and went through a severe detox."

xref.title: Remastering of "Pretty Hate Machine"
xref.body: Trent Reznor wished to remaster "Pretty Hate Machine" for the 21st century as 1989 studio technology was not as advanced as 2010. Legal disputes meant the original masters were inaccessible, causing the album to be out of print for years. In March 2010, The Bicycle Music Company acquired the rights and allowed Reznor to remaster it. The remastered version featured more forward vocals, greater clarity in arrangements, brighter piano, and reduced hiss. "But that changed in March of 2010 when the rights to the master recording were acquired by a company called the Bicycle Music Company. They allowed Trent access to these masters so he could remaster them."

xref.body: Trent Reznor later "returned the favor" to Jane's Addiction by getting involved in their reunion, recording songs with them, and touring together in the summer of 2009. xref.title: Small Town Perspective on Life and Music
xref.body: Trent Reznor articulated his experience growing up in small-town America, noting a limited scope of travel and the uniformity of amenities like Kmarts and movie theaters showing the same five Sylvester Stallone films. He felt playing music wasn't considered "cool" and that being in the band rather than the football team made you a "leper." "My scope of travel was maybe a half hour radius, and every town had the same Kmart and synoplex, all playing the same five movies, all Sylvester Stallone. It's hard for people who grow up in cities to understand that, to have an endless cornfield in your backyard. But that's what a lot of America is. It's not dodging gunfire from gangs. It wasn't cool to play music where I was, and I got a pretty bad education because I had a bad attitude. If I wanted to get good grades, I could. Stuff I'd like to know now, at the time, I thought was irrelevant. Typical teenage stupidity. I hated school. The fact that it revolved around something you didn't have access to. If you weren't on the football team and you were in the band, you were a leper. When people say those are the best years of our lives, I want to scream. But my parents allowed me to do things that my friends weren't allowed to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Solo Album with Trent Reznor - Unreleased
xref.body: After Rage Against the Machine disbanded in 2000, Zack De La Rocha began working on a solo record, delving into hip hop and freestyle rapping. He collaborated with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Reznor, who produced the material. Despite the material being considered "good" by Reznor, the album was never released and was shelved indefinitely for unknown reasons. "Rage was done by 2000... But Zach was determined to go solo. He got deep into hip hop and freestyle rapping and started working with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Rosner on a solo record. The material was good too, according to Trent anyway. But for a recent still unknown, the album was never released, shelved forever."

xref.body: As Trent Reznor's songwriting partner, Atticus Ross was given songwriting credits for Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road" following a quiet negotiation, sharing in the song's profits and Grammy wins. "Trent and his songwriting partner, Atticus Ross, were given songwriting credits on Old Town Road and thus a share of the profits."

xref.title: Songwriting Philosophy
xref.body: Trent Reznor's songwriting for "Pretty Hate Machine" and subsequent works was deeply rooted in honest, personal experience. Lacking a guitar-centric background, he utilized computers to simulate sounds, allowing him a broad sonic palette. He focused on relating his own feelings and dissatisfactions with relationships, religion, or government, disguising them to avoid preaching, aiming for relatability rather than political commentary. "So the only thing I could speak about with any authority was my own personal experience and tried to relate situations I'd been into or feelings I'd thought, or dissatisfactions with relationships or religion or the government of the country I live in, or whatever it is."

"Over time I think it was a matter of Zach not knowing what direction to go. xref.title: Trent Reznor's Addiction and Recovery
xref.body: After the last tour in 2001, Trent Reznor recognized he was at a breaking point due to alcoholism and addiction, which had consumed and destroyed him. Faced with a choice between death and recovery, he sought help and committed to turning his life around, realizing he wasn't ready to die. He began to focus on self-care, acknowledging his past reliance on self-medication to cope with early superstardom in the mid-90s. He had initially tried to address his addiction secretly in 1997 while recording 'The Fragile', believing he was cured upon its release, only to experience a severe relapse that lasted a year and a half and nearly cost him his life. His recovery journey involved learning humility, acknowledging his limitations, and taking time off to heal and reconnect with himself, all while fearing he might have lost his ability to write sober. "My soul had been crushed by being an alcoholic and an addict. And there was no denying at that point. And it had consumed me and destroyed me. And there was a fork in the road and it was either death by my own hand or from any number of other ways it could have happened or fix myself."

He felt this trend lacked originality and exploited a younger audience's unfamiliarity with the original artists who created the foundational sounds and aesthetics. "Generally, I've been pretty disgusted with music in the last several years. xref.title: Trilogy Chronological Interpretation
xref.body: Interpreting the trilogy backwards reveals Manson's autobiographical intent: starting as an untainted suburban individual (*Holy Wood*'s Adam Cadmon), then shaped by American culture (guns, God, government), rebelling by forming a band and engaging in depravity (*Mechanical Animals*' Omega), potentially with Trent Reznor as a mentor (Alpha), and finally emerging as a logical, unfeeling "survival of the fittest Superman" (*Antichrist Superstar*'s Antichrist Superstar). "All starts to make sense, don't I?"

xref.title: Uninspired by Trent Reznor Collaboration
